question: Can the PF coil cans carry effective toroidal resistivity above the seeded 0.90 micro-ohm metre bulk stainless bound?

edlington.title: Edlington, Martin and Pinfold, MAST magnetic diagnostics (2001)

berkery.title: Berkery et al., MAST conducting structure reconstruction

akers.title: Akers et al., First results from MAST (2001)

nist.title: Hust and Giarratano, NBS SRM 798 austenitic stainless steel
nist.locator: Table 4, p. 18 (PDF p. 30); units micro-ohm cm

claims.finding: The current provisional bulk austenitic stainless interval ends at 0.90 micro-ohm metre; the coil-can grade is explicitly undocumented.
The five non-solenoid PF coil pairs of original MAST were inside stainless steel cans; no alloy grade is named in the inspected machine description.
The cans were electrically connected to the vacuum vessel through both mechanical supports and feeder-bar vacuum bellows; those are additional current paths, not electrically isolated cans.
Case Rogowski measurements separated induced case current from feed current, and a later 3-D conducting-structure model compared a lower P4 case current with a MAST coil-test discharge.
The described insulating breaks prevent currents in diagnostic support rails. The passage does not locate a break in the PF coil cans.
An independently measured austenitic stainless reference sample has 0.811 micro-ohm metre at 300 K, 0.890 at 400 K and 0.923 at 450 K; it is not identified as MAST can stock.
A MAST report gives 200 C designed and 140 C achieved bake-out temperatures. These are vessel bake values, not coil-can temperatures during the held-out vacuum shots.

Linear interpolation of the reference sample between 400 and 450 K crosses 0.90 micro-ohm metre at about 415 K (142 C). This is an illustrative material threshold, not a measured MAST operating condition.
The MAST source says stainless steel without a grade; no source reviewed identifies a higher-resistivity grade in these cans.

claims.hypothesis: higher temperature during the fitted shots
claims.finding: The reference alloy could exceed 0.90 micro-ohm metre near 142 C, but the MAST source gives only bake-out temperatures and no can temperature for the fitted shots.

No can seam or electrical segmentation is specified. The explicit insulating breaks belong to diagnostic rails; observed case currents do not establish whether each case is a closed ring or closes through the vessel.

The MAST cans have two documented electrical connections to the vessel, and a 3-D vessel-and-cases model is used to estimate effective reduced resistances. The sign and size of this path's bias in the current held-out fit remain unmeasured.

The reviewed sources do not establish a coil-case bulk resistivity above 0.90 micro-ohm metre at the fitted shot temperature or a quantified segmentation multiplier. The provisional bound therefore stays unchanged; vessel-coupled topology is a supported model-extension candidate.
